newsitem.title: GERMANY: German emergency savings package takes shape.
newsitem.headline: German emergency savings package takes shape.

text.p: A German government emergency savings package began to take shape on Wednesday as Finance Minister Theo Waigel prepared for bad news in the form of a sharp shortfall in expected tax revenues this year.

Waigel told journalists he was already thinking of higher net borrowing and selling some of Bonn's shares in Deutsche Telekom AG to help fight a growing budget deficit threatening Germany's chances to qualify for Europe's single currency.

Details of the savings package were not expected to be known until late on Thursday, after the tax estimate figure is announced and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right government submits the plan to its parliamentary deputies for approval.

Coalition officials say the tax revenue projection undershoots previous estimates by almost 20 billion marks, with roughly eight billion missing in federal taxes, eight billion in the states and the rest in cities and towns.

In addition, Bonn faces extra costs of about six billion marks for the Federal Labour Office, which pays unemployment benefits and retrains workers. German joblessness is running at a record 4.1 million average this year.
Coalition members said several savings measures were under discussion, including:

--- Higher Net Borrowing: Germany's overall 1997 public borrowing, including that of its federal states, is due to reach 99.5 billion marks. Federal borrowing accounts for 53.3 billion of that figure. Waigel said borrowing would have to be higher because of Germany's continuing record unemployment.

Germany could borrow more than planned this year and still meet the Maastricht deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product, government officials say, because the planned overall deficit this year amounts to only 2.5 percent of GDP.
The three percent ceiling would stand somewhere between 108 and 115 billion marks, depending on how it is calculated.

--- Telekom shares: Bonn is considering selling some of its shares in Deutsche Telekom, of which it owns 74 percent. German law currently bars Bonn from selling shares on the stock market until the year 2000. But Bonn could transfer some holdings to the Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau as it did with its remaining Lufthansa shares last year.

--- Budget Savings: Some of the Federal Labour Office retraining schemes could be eliminated, the officials said. A general spending freeze for all federal ministries is also being considered. Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Wednesday he had no room for any more cuts in his budget.

--- Boosting Tax Revenues: The Free Democratic Party (FDP), Kohl's small liberal coalition partner, said on Wednesday that any measure was better than tax increases. Waigel also effectively ruled out tax rises . Officials said Bonn could bring in more tax revenue by deciding to tax hidden reserves the power utility companies put aside to pay for mothballing nuclear power plants. Der Spiegel magazine said last month that could bring in another 1.5 to three billion marks.
The government's "Tax Estimate Working Group" met for a second day of closed-door deliberations in the eastern city of Schwerin on Wednesday.

The group is made up of about two dozen officials from the federal and state finance ministries, the federal economics ministry, the leading economic research institutes, Bonn's economic advisory panel, the Bundesbank central bank, the Federal Statistics Office and the association of German cities.

After presenting their revenue estimates for various types of taxes, they work out a consensus estimate of the overall revenue total which in the past has proved to be correct to about one percent of the amount finally taken in.
